item.passage:
The anniversary party was in the backyard of the house on Crane Road, where Lena's grandparents had lived for forty years, and Lena had been asked to give the first toast. She had written it a week before: three jokes about her grandfather's terrible singing and one line about how her grandmother could still beat anyone in the family at checkers.

On the morning of the party, she came in from setting up chairs and heard her grandmother on the kitchen phone. "We'll tell everyone tonight, after the cake," Grandma Rosa was saying. "It's time somebody else had the house. Forty years is long enough for two people to rattle around in it."

Lena backed out through the screen door before anyone saw her. She walked slowly around the yard, past the pear tree she had fallen out of at seven, the cellar door with its rusted handle, and the little cottage at the back of the lot that had stood empty since before she was born. By the time she reached the porch, she had decided the jokes were wrong. Nobody should joke about singing on the last summer in a house.

She sat on the back steps and wrote a new toast on the back of a paper plate.

When her father tapped his glass at six o'clock, she stood and read it. She described the pear tree and the cellar door. She described the third stair, which creaked so loudly that nobody had ever come home late without being caught, and the kitchen window where Grandpa Joe kept a row of tomatoes ripening on the sill. She said that whoever lived here next would be getting a good house, and she hoped they would know what they had.

When she sat down, the yard was quiet. Her mother was looking at her father. Grandma Rosa had put a hand over her mouth. Grandpa Joe's shoulders were shaking, and it took Lena a moment to understand that he was laughing.

He crossed the lawn and sat beside her on the step. "Who told you we were selling?"

She told him about the phone call.

"Your grandmother was talking to your aunt," he said. "We're moving into the cottage out back, where there's one floor and no stairs. The house goes to your mother and father. They have known since spring; that was the news for after the cake." He tapped the paper plate. "By September you'll be sleeping right over that creaky stair."

Lena looked down at the plate, at her list of everything she had been trying to memorize. Her face was hot.

"Keep it," Grandpa Joe said. "Somebody in this family should have written that down years ago. Next year, though, put in the jokes about my singing. I was looking forward to those."

The chairs are upside down on the desks,
thirty pairs of legs held up toward the ceiling
like a class that knows every answer
with no one left to call on.

I have come in to take down the posters,
and the light has gotten here before me,
lying in long panes across the floor,
the dust turning slowly through it
the way small fish turn in a tank.

On the board, the last lesson was erased
in wide gray loops, but the chalk held on
the way a footprint stays in packed sand:
I can still read Equator, and beneath it
a date in June, and an arrow pointing nowhere.

The clock above the door keeps running.
The pencil sharpener holds a little drift
of cedar shavings that smell, when I lift the lid,
like a morning in March.

For nine months I stood at the front of this room.
Today I lift a chair down from the back row
and sit in it, and the room turns around:

the board is a pale square, half lost in glare,
my desk is small and far away,
and to the left, filling the whole window,
is the maple by the bus loop,
every leaf of it moving.

So that is where they were looking
all those afternoons I thought they had drifted.
They were watching the wind arrive
in the top branches first,
then the middle, then the low ones by the glass,
a little before it reached the room.

I sit there longer than I meant to.
Then I take down the posters,
and on the first page of next year's plan book
I write, before anything else:
turn the desks toward the window.

In my first season on the junior varsity volleyball team, I could not serve. I could hit the ball, and hard, which was exactly the trouble. My serves sailed into the back wall of the gym or drove into the bottom of the net, and on bad days they did both in the same game. By October our coach had begun taking me out whenever my turn to serve came around.

Marisol Vega was a senior and the best server in our league, and one afternoon after practice she asked me to stay. I expected advice about my arm. Instead she handed me a ball and told me to toss it, just toss it, and let it fall.

"Higher," she said. "And out in front of your right shoulder, not behind your head." I tossed it again. "Again." I tossed it forty times that day without a single swing. She watched each ball land and pointed with her foot to where it had come down, and the spots were scattered over a circle as wide as a doormat.

I thought this was a waste of an afternoon, and I said so. Marisol shrugged. "You think your serve goes wrong when you hit it," she said. "It goes wrong before that. If the ball is somewhere different every time, your arm has to fix it every time, and it can't."

For two weeks I came early and tossed. I put a strip of tape on the gym floor a little in front of my right foot and tried to make the ball land on it. At first maybe one toss in ten did. By the second week it was most of them, and I had begun to feel the toss in my fingers instead of following it with my eyes: a soft lift with the flat of the hand, the ball barely turning as it rose.

Only then did Marisol let me hit. She taught me to strike the ball with the heel of my hand, wrist stiff, and to stop my arm short instead of following through, so that the ball left my hand without spin. A ball without spin, she explained, catches the air unevenly and wobbles on its way over the net, and the player waiting for it cannot tell until the last moment which way it will dip.

My first serve like that went in during a game in November. It dipped at the last second, the girl receiving it put her forearms out in the wrong place, and the ball dropped to the floor beside her. Our bench made a noise I can still hear.

I have taught that serve to younger players since, and I always start where Marisol started, with the ball and the tape and no hitting at all. Most of them think it is a waste of an afternoon. I let them say so. The hard part of a serve comes before the part everyone watches, and that is something you learn with your hands, by tossing, long before you believe it.

In 1884 the eleven farming settlements strung along the upper Tallis River shared a single doctor, who reached them on horseback. Dr. Amos Fenwick had come to the valley from a city practice at the age of thirty-four, answering an advertisement placed by the settlement of Corby Mills. It promised him a house, a horse, and a salary of four hundred dollars a year, raised by subscription among the families of the town. Within two years the other settlements had joined the subscription, and Fenwick's practice covered nearly sixty miles of river road.

He could not be everywhere at once, so in 1886 the valley settled on a system. Fenwick rode the full length of the river road every nine days, upstream on one trip and down on the next. A household that needed him tied a strip of red cloth to its gatepost, and he stopped at every gate that showed one. Neighbors kept an eye on the gates along their stretch of road; if a farm far from the road raised a cloth, someone carried word down to the river and tied a second strip where Fenwick would see it.

The system had obvious limits. A child who fell ill the morning after the doctor passed might wait more than a week, and in emergencies families still sent a rider after him, sometimes chasing his route for a full day before catching up. Fenwick's daybook, which survives in the county historical collection, records one winter in which he saw patients on fifty-one days in a row and slept in his own bed on nine of them.

Still, the cloths changed what a doctor could do in the valley. Before them, families sent for help only when an illness seemed desperate, because fetching a doctor cost a day's work and often brought him too late. A strip of cloth cost almost nothing, and it asked only that a family judge, every few days, whether someone in the house was getting worse. Fenwick's daybook shows the effect. In his first two years, before the cloths, most of his visits were to patients already gravely ill; by his sixth year, more than half were to cuts, coughs, and fevers caught early, when there was more he could do.

The red cloths came down in 1903, when the valley opened a twelve-bed hospital in a former grain warehouse at Corby Mills and two younger doctors joined Fenwick there. A telephone line along the river road followed four years later. Fenwick, by then nearly sixty, gave up the circuit and took the night shift at the hospital, which he kept until he retired.

Older residents of the valley used the phrase for decades afterward. A neighbor who looked unwell might be told, half seriously, that it was time to hang out the red cloth, meaning that it was time to stop waiting and ask for help.

Dr. Amos Fenwick had come to the valley from a city practice at the age of thirty-four, answering an advertisement placed by the settlement of Corby Mills. It promised him a house, a horse, and a salary of four hundred dollars a year, raised by subscription among the families of the town. Within two years the other settlements had joined the subscription, and Fenwick's practice covered nearly sixty miles of river road.

He could not be everywhere at once, so in 1886 the valley settled on a system. Fenwick rode the full length of the river road every nine days, upstream on one trip and down on the next. A household that needed him tied a strip of red cloth to its gatepost, and he stopped at every gate that showed one. Neighbors kept an eye on the gates along their stretch of road; if a farm far from the road raised a cloth, someone carried word down to the river and tied a second strip where Fenwick would see it.

The system had obvious limits. A child who fell ill the morning after the doctor passed might wait more than a week, and in emergencies families still sent a rider after him, sometimes chasing his route for a full day before catching up. Fenwick's daybook, which survives in the county historical collection, records one winter in which he saw patients on fifty-one days in a row and slept in his own bed on nine of them.

Still, the cloths changed what a doctor could do in the valley. Before them, families sent for help only when an illness seemed desperate, because fetching a doctor cost a day's work and often brought him too late. A strip of cloth cost almost nothing, and it asked only that a family judge, every few days, whether someone in the house was getting worse. Fenwick's daybook shows the effect. In his first two years, before the cloths, most of his visits were to patients already gravely ill; by his sixth year, more than half were to cuts, coughs, and fevers caught early, when there was more he could do.

The red cloths came down in 1903, when the valley opened a twelve-bed hospital in a former grain warehouse at Corby Mills and two younger doctors joined Fenwick there. A telephone line along the river road followed four years later. Fenwick, by then nearly sixty, gave up the circuit and took the night shift at the hospital, which he kept until he retired.

item.passage:
For an animal that may see the world without color, the cuttlefish is remarkably good at matching it. Its eyes appear to contain only one kind of light-sensitive pigment, which in most animals would mean an inability to tell red from green or blue from yellow. Yet a cuttlefish set down on reddish gravel or among green weed will, within seconds, take on a pattern that blends with its surroundings. How it manages this is a question biologists are still working on, and the answer seems to lie partly in its skin and partly in what it pays attention to.

The skin itself works something like a screen. Near its surface lie enormous numbers of tiny elastic sacs called chromatophores, each holding yellow, red, or brown pigment. Each sac is ringed by small muscles connected to nerves that run from the brain. When the muscles contract, they pull the sac open and spread its color over a wider patch of skin; when they relax, the sac shrinks back to a speck. Because the brain works these muscles directly, rather than through hormones carried slowly in the blood, a cuttlefish can redraw its pattern in a fraction of a second.

Beneath the chromatophores lie layers of cells that reflect light instead of absorbing it. Some, called iridophores, produce shimmering blues and greens, much as a thin film of oil on water does. Others, called leucophores, scatter all colors of light about evenly and so look white. Because these white cells reflect whatever light falls on them, they may help explain the puzzle: they can tint the animal toward the colors around it without the cuttlefish needing to see those colors at all.

What the cuttlefish does seem to judge closely is brightness and pattern. In a well-known series of experiments, researchers placed young cuttlefish on checkerboards of black and white squares. On boards with very small squares, the animals turned a fine mottle. On boards whose squares were roughly the size of a white patch on the cuttlefish's own body, they produced bold blocks of light and dark that broke up their outline. On a plain gray surface they turned a nearly even shade. Researchers now sort most cuttlefish camouflage into these three broad types: uniform, mottled, and disruptive.

Hiding is only part of the story, because cuttlefish also use their skin to be seen. A hunting cuttlefish will sometimes send dark bands rippling across its body toward its prey, a display researchers call "passing clouds," which may startle a crab into holding still. Males courting females put on high-contrast striped displays, and in one Australian species, smaller males have been observed hiding their male markings and taking on the look of females to slip past larger rivals.

The skin, then, is better thought of as a display than as a disguise alone, and the animal can switch it in an instant from "I am gravel" to "look at me." Biologists are still testing how much of what the cuttlefish sees it can turn into pattern, and how it does so with eyes that, as far as anyone can tell, cannot see color.
